newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bezeq workers return but Israeli phones still down.
newsitem.headline: Bezeq workers return but Israeli phones still down.

text.p: Employees of state-owned Bezeq Israel Telecom returned to work on Wednesday but refused to comply fully with a labour court order to restore normal telephone services, union and company officials said.

Bezeq workers went on strike last week over government plans to privatise more of the company, which is 76 percent state-owned, through the $250 million sale of 12.5 percent of its stock to Merrill Lynch.
"Workers returned to work but work is not proceeding at its usual pace," Bezeq labour union spokesman Tzvi Vilnai said. "The workers are very disturbed, very troubled.
"The Merrill Lynch move is the main problem," he said.
The strike at Israel's main telecommunications provider left thousands of homes and businesses without full telephone services and forced the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange to halt trading on Tuesday.
Disruption continued on Wednesday, with many lines down, though the exchange reopened for business. Bezeq's own stock was trading at 9.95 shekels, down from 10.0 at the previous close.
Bezeq director-general Ami Harel said management had again turned to a labour court to try to force workers to restore normal services.

On Tuesday, the Tel Aviv Labour Court ordered Bezeq workers to return immediately to their jobs and begin negotiations with the Government Corporations Authority, which oversees privatisation, and the Communications Ministry.

The Merrill Lynch deal involves 90.6 million shares, or 12.5 percent of Bezeq stock. The first tranche of 2.5 percent of shares is being sold for $50 million, or 5 percent below the market value on July 10. Merrill Lynch cannot return these shares to the government.

An additional 10 percent is being sold at market value for $200 million. Merrill Lynch has five months from Sept. 1 to sell these shares to its clients. The government has agreed to buy back any stock from this package that remains unsold.

Union leaders said the deal violated government promises to involve Bezeq workers in all aspects of the company's privatisation and called for the sale to be cancelled or to use its revenues to fund early pension programmes.
The government has already floated 24 percent of Bezeq but in 1995, Britain's Cable & Wireless PLC bought up about 10 percent of the public float on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
Further share offerings have been delayed while Cable and the government seek to determine Cable's future role at Bezeq.
